K(R) — curvature coefficient (Theorem 2), numerical estimate

TheoremNumerical estimate
VR(φ) = VR(0) + K(R)·φ² + o(φ²), K(R)>0 for every R>1

For a transfer angle close to 180°, the cost behaves as VR(φ) ≈ VR(0) + K·φ², where K depends only on the radius ratio R=r₂/r₁ (Theorem 2's closed-form coefficient — this chart estimates it numerically from the exact engine for a sweep of R, the same way every other live quantity in this demo is computed). K>0 everywhere is exactly what makes Δθ=180° a genuine local minimum for every R>1, not just the one currently selected. The dot marks the R you've set above.

Asymptotic check — the quadratic law of Theorem 2

TheoremNumerical check
VR(φ) = VR(0) + K(R)·φ² + o(φ²), K(R)>0 for every R>1

Two direct, quantitative checks of VR(φ) = VR(0) + K·φ² + O(φ⁴) as φ→0, for the R currently set above — not just a parabola drawn by eye, but the two quantities the asymptotic claim is actually about.

Top: the ratio [VR(φ)−VR(0)]/φ², which the claim says converges to the constant K(R) (dashed line) as φ→0 — not to some other value, and not diverging.

Bottom: the residual VR(φ)−VR(0)−K·φ² left over once the quadratic term is subtracted off, on a log scale — it should fall away much faster than φ² itself as φ→0, which is what "+O(φ⁴)" means. The flattening at the smallest φ shown is the floating-point noise floor of this in-browser engine, not a feature of the theorem.

Near the Hohmann angle the cost landscape in p is genuinely very sharp — a ±20% band in p would print enormous, real but hard-to-read numbers here, so a much narrower band is sampled instead. Move the angle slider further from 180° to see the gentler, broader valley shown in the reference figures.

Independent validation

A single solver can have a bug that its own answer would never reveal. Three independent methods below each compute the same orbit a completely different way, live in your browser, every time you change an input.

This matters specifically because the paper behind this demo claims an exact, provable minimum — not just a plausible number. An unnoticed bug in a single optimizer could silently produce a wrong Δv that still looked reasonable. Cross-checking it against two unrelated methods (closed-form geometry and step-by-step numerical integration) is what turns "this looks right" into "this is verified right."

1. Geometry check

Re-derives the orbit from angular-momentum conservation and the vis-viva equation — independently of the optimizer.

—

2. Lambert cross-check

A separate classical method (universal-variable Lambert solver), fed this transfer's own time of flight, recovers the same orbit from scratch.

—

3. RK4 numerical propagation

Integrates the equations of motion step by step from the departure state and compares to the known arrival state — shares no formulas with either check above.

—

    How Theorems 1–4 Fit Together

    Four results about one function, VR(φ) — read top to bottom, or click any card to expand it.

    1. The function
    2. Growth away from Hohmann
    3. Curvature / shape
    4. Why there is no contradiction

    The function

    For a fixed radius ratio R=r₂/r₁>1, VR(φ) is the minimum Δv needed to go from a circular orbit of radius r₁ to one of radius r₂, written as a function of the angular deviation φ from the direct Hohmann transfer (φ=0 at Δθ=180°). Every result below describes how this one function behaves — nothing else changes between them.

    φ = |Δθ − 180°| · π/180, R = r₂/r₁ > 1

    Growth away from Hohmann

    Does the cost ever go back down, the farther you get from the direct transfer?

    Theorem 2 — local quadratic law

    ▾
    Theorem
    VR(φ) = VR(0) + K(R)·φ² + o(φ²), K(R)>0 for every radius ratio R>1

    Right at Hohmann, the cost rises quadratically — a strict local minimum.

    The coefficient K(R) is given in closed form and is proved strictly positive for every radius ratio. This rules out the alternative that Δθ=180° could be a flat point or a saddle — it is a genuine, strict local minimum, for every R>1 without exception.

    ↓local minimum → global minimum

    Theorem 1 — global monotonicity

    ▾
    Theorem
    VR(φ) strictly increasing in φ ∈ (0°,180°), for every radius ratio R>1

    The local behavior extends all the way: cost only ever increases, moving away from Hohmann, on the whole range.

    Not just near φ=0: over the entire admissible angular range, for every radius ratio, moving away from the Hohmann configuration — on either side — strictly increases the cost, with no exception and no region where it levels off or decreases again. This makes Δθ=180° the unique global optimum, not merely a local one.

    Curvature / shape

    Does the curvature keep a constant sign throughout, or can it change along the way?

    Theorem 3 — global convexity in z

    ▾
    Theorem
    d²VR/dz² > 0 for all z>0, every radius ratio R>1 (z=cot²(φ/2))

    Reparametrized in z=cot²(φ/2), the curve is strictly convex over its entire domain — it never changes curvature.

    This is a stronger, more structural statement than monotonicity: it says how the slope itself evolves, not just its sign. It holds over the whole domain, for every radius ratio R>1, with no exception at any particular ratio — proved via an exact algebraic reduction to a polynomial sign-check, certified rather than numerically sampled.

    same underlying shape, read on two different rulers — not a contradiction, see below ↓

    Theorem 4 — curvature inflection in φ

    ▾
    Theorem
    d²VR/dφ² changes sign exactly once, at φc≈164.37° (R=2 only)

    Viewed directly in the angle φ rather than in z, the same underlying behavior shows a curvature sign change — proved exactly for R=2.

    This does not contradict Theorem 3. Convexity in z and a curvature sign change in φ are two valid descriptions of the same underlying behavior, taken with two different scales on the horizontal axis: z=cot²(φ/2) is a monotonic but non-affine change of variable, so it can turn a one-way bend in z into a curvature sign change in φ. Certified over the entire admissible interval for R=2, using four complementary methods whose ranges of application overlap.

    Open question — does this generalize beyond R=2?

    ▾
    Open / conjecture

    Whether Theorem 4's curvature sign change occurs for every radius ratio R>1, or only for R=2, is not yet settled.

    This is Conjecture 2 in the manuscript. Numerical exploration across a range of radius ratios is consistent with the same curvature sign change persisting beyond R=2, but no certified proof covers the general case yet — this remains active, unfinished work.

    Why there is no contradiction

    Theorem 1 describes the sign of the slope of VR(φ): it only ever goes up, moving away from Hohmann. Theorems 3 and 4 describe the sign of the curvature — a completely different property. A function can be strictly increasing from end to end while still changing curvature somewhere in the middle: the two statements are about different derivatives, so neither one limits the other.

    Together, the four results replace an intuition orbital engineers already had informally — "the cost grows and behaves simply away from Hohmann" — with a general proof, valid without exception, and they expose a genuinely counter-intuitive fact: a strictly monotonic cost can still change its curvature along the way. All four are established the same way, by exact algebraic reduction and certified polynomial sign-checking, not by numerical sampling — see the tabs for the full derivations.
